summary:
Bahrain decriminalised same-sex sexual activity in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era statute, and is the only Gulf state that does not explicitly penalise same-sex intimacy. No statute criminalises transgender expression. Under the 1976 penal code the age of adulthood for consensual same-sex acts is 21.

Decriminalisation has not removed exposure. Authorities continue to bring morality and indecency charges under Articles 324, 329 and 350 of the penal code, which carry three months to two years' imprisonment, fines up to 200 Bahraini dinars, and deportation for non-Bahrainis. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a hotel discotheque party in Manama on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. A man received a one-month sentence in 2009 for wearing an abaya and carrying a purse in public, and police raided a 2011 party described as a same-sex wedding. In February 2024 the Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation, extending the framework under which such charges are brought.

Entry is screened on gender presentation. The Interior Minister has stated that suspected effeminate homosexuals are barred from entering Bahrain through airport checks, and pending bills have proposed expressly banning LGBTQ foreigners from entry or from residency permits. In September 2013 the Gulf Cooperation Council agreed to discuss a proposal to test and exclude gay foreigners, though officials later backtracked.

Legal gender recognition is refused by the courts. In a May 2023 judgment a lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia, and refused his request for a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination. A 2023 ruling held sex-reassignment procedures contrary to Islamic law where a case is considered solely related to gender dysphoria, limiting eligibility to people with intersex traits. Courts require medical documentation of a sex change operation or of medical necessity before a legal marker is changed.

Gender-affirming medical care is heavily restricted. Article 330 of the penal code requires anyone charged with prostitution or fujoor to be taken to a hospital for sexually transmitted disease testing and permits relocation to a medical facility.

No law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and no hate-crime protection extends to gender and sexual minorities.
tangentialFactors:
Legislative proposals remain live. A bill tabled in October 2021 would have criminalised promoting or inviting others to homosexual gatherings with up to five years' imprisonment, and other pending bills would instruct teachers to identify warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing so that children can be disciplined. The pending entry and residency bans on LGBTQ foreigners belong to the same legislative stream.

False accusations of homosexuality are used to discredit and bully government critics and protesters, including human-rights advocate Nabeel Rajab and demonstrators at Pearl Square in 2011. The charge functions as a reputational instrument independent of any conduct.

Media hostility is open and unremedied. A widely viewed Albilad caricature published on 3 August 2024 depicted a pride-flag roll of toilet paper captioned 'the correct place'. Article 309 of the penal code protects religious groups but extends no equivalent protection to LGBTQ people, so hate speech against the community circulates without legal consequence.
localsOnly:
The Education Ministry disclaims responsibility for sexuality issues. Assistant Under-Secretary for Educational Services Khalid Al Alawi stated that addressing sexuality is parents' job and that 'The public shouldn't make a big deal out of this problem because it does not exist', while adding that students whose appearance is contrary to school values should be disciplined.

On 14 February 2024 the Ministry of Education referred a private school's administration and its entire board to investigation and dismissed the general manager after a video showed two male students pretending to propose to each other in class. A 2022 incident, in which a private school distributed material perceived as promoting homosexuality, also prompted calls for stricter laws. The Gulf Daily News has run articles on female homosexuality in girls' high schools.

No LGBTQ-specific facilities, shelters or community organisations exist. The US Department of State reports that no LGBTQ-related organisations are approved, and ILGA concludes that registration of a sexual- or gender-diversity group is improbable because the body controlling association registration may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved conflict in the sources. Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada response RIO BHR105575.E of August 2016 reports that 'according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain', citing a Canadian government update of 14 July 2016 and Gulf News of 5 February 2011. That reading contradicts the 1976-decriminalisation position carried by Wikipedia, Outright International and the 2023 US State Department report, and the inventory does not reconcile the two.

Verification is constrained. Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade, including United Nations human-rights bodies and Amnesty International, so local media often serve as the only source for this jurisdiction.

The status of the pending bills is not sourced: whether the October 2021 promotion bill, the proposed entry and residency bans, and the teacher-instruction bills were enacted, lapsed or remain before the legislature is unresolved in the inventory.
